slides.say: For every positive integer x, the double bracket of x is the number of times five appears in the prime factorization of x. For example, fifty is two times five times five, it has two fives, so the double bracket of fifty is two. Which of the following must be true?

slides: This question mixes a new operation with prime factors. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, plugging in a number, and then by understanding.

slides.say: [short pause] A definition in words is easy to misread, so let's see it in numbers first. Fifty is two times five times five, so it has two fives. Seventy-five is three times five times five, two fives as well. And seven has no fives at all, so its count is zero.

Now let's plug in the simplest value, x is one. One has no fives, so its count is zero. Choice number one says: the double bracket of five x equals the double bracket of x squared. Five times one is five, which has one five. One squared is one, with no fives. One is not zero, so choice number one is out. Choice number two says: the double bracket of x plus five equals the double bracket of x, plus one. One plus five is six, and six is two times three, no fives, so zero. On the right, zero plus one is one. Zero is not one, out. Choice number three says: the double bracket of five x equals five times the double bracket of x. Five has one five, but five times zero is zero. One is not zero, out.
at: double bracket of five x equals five

slides.say: Choice number four says: the double bracket of five x equals the double bracket of x, plus one. Five has one five, and zero plus one is one. One equals one. Three choices are out, so choice number four is our answer.

[pause] Now by understanding. Let's see why it's always true. When we multiply x by five, we add exactly one more five to its prime factors, whatever x is. So the count of fives goes up by exactly one. That's choice number four, for every x. For example, fifty has two fives, and two hundred fifty has three.
at: we add exactly one more five

slides.say: The others are not always true, and x is one already showed that. So choice number four is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
